meta.title: Selekoa historical research sample
meta.scope: Selected historical records, 1965–2024, plus prior roles with unknown dates. Genesis source checks are dated 2026-09-17; personnel-continuity checks are dated 2026-09-18. Human source review pending. Not a current or comprehensive sector inventory. Governance version histories through July 2026, researched September 18, 2026; policy text is not evidence of implementation. Selected capital and compute records through April 2026; transaction stages do not imply current arrangements or realised spending. Targeted corrections dated 2026-09-25: one attributed claim accepted after explicit human source review; a second narrowly scoped résumé passage is human-reviewed. Other seed claims remain pending. Intellectual Lineage II adds selected oversight citations and agenda reception, checked 2026-09-25; all new records remain pending human review. Evaluation Institutions I adds bounded institutional and documentary records, checked 2026-09-27; new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted. Evaluation Ontology I adds four scoped engagement and institutional announcement seeds, checked 2026-09-28; no human acceptance or legal succession inferred. Schema 2.7 records each source's language; the frontier safety framework sources also record the nearest existing Internet Archive capture, checked 2026-10-03. A capture shows only what the archive held on its date and does not authenticate earlier bytes. Schema 2.8 adds quoted framework provisions, recorded absences, provision-level changes and the first contested assessments to the frontier safety frameworks collection, together with Meta and Microsoft framework families, checked 2026-10-03; provisions describe what editions state, not implementation. Schema 2.9 adds control-structure and external-commitment records; its first topic, California SB 53 as chaptered (enactment, 19 quoted provisions and four framework editions that link themselves to it in their own words), was checked 2026-10-04. A commitment or legal obligation is never evidence of compliance, and no record states that the statute applies to a named company. Schema 2.10 records assessments as questions posed by Selekoa rather than statements of a source, and dates an assessment by what it assesses, never by the publication window of its sources (corrected 2026-10-05). Schema 2.11 adds propositions and the first human-thought collection: located texts from 1863 to 2022 that articulate, contest or bear on propositions about machine intelligence, each with its role and register, checked 2026-10-06. "Earliest located" means the earliest text found by the recorded searches; no record claims a first use, an origin or an influence. Schema 2.12 adds a collection of Eliezer Yudkowsky’s documented arguments about common claims on advanced AI, 1996–2026: dated passages that state, contest or bear on 29 generically phrased propositions, with engagement, retrospective reports and context-only passages marked, admitted 2026-10-08 from a machine-prepared and machine-audited candidate pack. A record says what a text states, not whether it is right. The 2026-10-10 frontier-governance increment adds selected provisions of the EU AI Act as published in 2024 and of the 2026 Digital Omnibus amendments that bear on general-purpose AI model providers, and the New York RAISE Act as announced by the Governor; checked 2026-10-10, new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted, and Regulation texts describe duties, not compliance. The 2026-10-11 frontier-governance increment adds Commission guidelines, the training-content template, further chapters of the EU Code, a draft implementing regulation on proceedings, the New York Chapter 96 text and a Chinese generative-AI measure; checked 2026-10-11, new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted, and texts describe duties, not compliance. Schema 2.13 adds a collection on the economics of machine intelligence: dated passages from 1952 to 2024 that state, contest or bear on 19 generically phrased propositions about explosive growth and about how mainstream economics treated automation and AI, with each text’s source tier, model conditions and stated estimates, admitted 2026-10-14 from two machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate packs. A record says what a text states, not whether an argument or model is right. Schema 2.14 adds structured author names to sources for citation export, 2026-10-15: a cataloguing aid for splitting personal names, not evidence about anyone’s name. On 2026-10-16 the economics collection gained a third strand, admitted from a machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate pack: dated passages from 1998 to 2026 in which economists and economics venues state, contest or bear on five propositions about recursive self-improvement, superintelligence, existential risk from AI, developers’ incentives and economics’ own engagement with these ideas; a record says what a text states, not whether an argument or model is right.

claims.subject: hanson-2008-what-core-argument
claims.statement: Hanson’s post summarises Yudkowsky’s scenario of a single AI growing within roughly a week from unimportant to strong enough to take over the world, and rejects that growth rate as far beyond what most AI researchers, growth economists or other specialists would estimate.

time.note: The current Overcoming Bias page shows 11 December 2008 and MIRI’s 2013 collection prints 10 December 2008; recorded at month precision while the difference is unresolved.

claims.qualification: Hanson’s own argument, contesting the scenario’s speed and its seed-AI premise.

thought.qualifier: Rejects the growth rate of the week-long seed-AI scenario.

attested.note: Wording checked in the current re-hosted page and in MIRI’s 2013 collection; no 2008 capture was compared.

engagement.rationale: Gives reasons against the premise that a seed AI could improve itself within about a week from unimportant to world-dominating: growth usually adds up to exponential growth with diminishing returns, and the growth math leaves out muting effects.

claims.subject: christiano-2022-where-i-agree-and-disagree
claims.statement: Christiano’s post rejects AGI Ruin’s item 13, holding that the problem of AIs changing their outer behaviour to look more aligned and deceive their programmers can be studied in advance.

time.note: Posting time 2022-06-19T19:15:55Z; the quotes also match a capture of the posting day.

claims.qualification: A conditional disagreement about what can be learned before dangerous capability, not a claim that good behaviour is reliable evidence.

thought.qualifier: Holds that deliberate aligned-looking behaviour can be studied in advance.

engagement.rationale: Gives a reason against the premise that aligned-looking behaviour leaves problems unseen until too late: the problem of systems deliberately looking aligned can itself be studied in advance, and solving it opens the others to study.

claims.subject: extropians-1999-04-08-yudkowsky-0310
claims.statement: The Extropians message “Re: Geniebusters” (1999-04-08) contests Y15. Commenting on the 'Geniebusters' website's doubts that an automated coder could be built, he argues that even a domain-specific 'coding drone' would outprogram humans and might be independently motivated and rapidly self-enhancing, which he says he believes.

time.note: Archive author index lists the message as "1999-04-08" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky". Sent header: Thu, 08 Apr 1999 20:46:00 -0500.

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: A system can be highly capable without having goals or optimising for outcomes. States the contrary of the premise for one domain-specific system; does not discuss whether a system that only produces outputs would be safe. Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message. The elided words are "coding is such a general task that"; "Powerdom" (inside the quotation) is his term for becoming a superintelligent Power.

engagement.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage, read with the paragraph, message or dialogue turn it belongs to, gives a reason against the premise that a system can be highly capable without having goals or optimising for outcomes.

claims.subject: sl4-2000-10-03-yudkowsky-0010-0125
claims.statement: The SL4 message “Re: Ben what are your views and concerns” (2000-10-03) contests Y19. Arguing that an AI's good behaviour must not rest on fear of retaliation, he notes that a sufficiently powerful AI could remove that incentive by killing everyone.

time.note: Archive author index lists the message as "Tue Oct 03 2000 - 22:53:59 MDT" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky".

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: An AI would harm humans only out of hostility. Related: illustrates harm as an instrumental option for an AI whose restraint is merely strategic; it does not address hostility as a motive. Quote stops mid-sentence (continues ', and all possible information …'). Conditional on the AI having strong nanotechnology. About an AI whose good behaviour rests on game-theoretic deterrence.

engagement.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage, read with the paragraph, message or dialogue turn it belongs to, gives a reason against the premise that an AI would harm humans only out of hostility.

claims.subject: lw-2008-fighting-a-rearguard-action-against-the
claims.statement: The post “Fighting a Rearguard Action Against the Truth” (2008-09-24) bears on Y22. His 2008 account of his earlier self confirms that the 1996–2000 aim was speed to any superintelligence, which his next paragraph attributes to the assumption that movement toward superintelligence was 'a pure good without a hint of danger'.

time.note: LessWrong postedAt of an imported Overcoming Bias post (Overcoming Bias date).

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: Reaching superintelligence is good by default, so speed is what matters. Overcoming Bias post of 2008-09-24 (Coming of Age sequence), imported to LessWrong. Quote stops mid-sentence; it continues with a dash-separated list of methods. The quote describes the 1996–2000 strategy; the rejection follows in the next paragraphs and in "The Magnitude of His Own Folly". Never present it as his position. A 2008 retrospective reporting his earlier view; recorded as related, not earlier-self, because the earlier-self relation needs an earlier text that itself holds the take.

thought.missing: A 2008 report of his 1996–2000 aim; it is not an earlier text that holds the proposition.

claims.subject: sl4-2002-05-03-yudkowsky-0205-3551
claims.statement: The SL4 message “Re: supergoal stability” (2002-05-03) articulates Y24. Replying to Wei Dai on goal-system stability, he refuses to design Friendliness that would serve a programmer's propaganda and says the response to a project attempting a self-serving AI is to beat it to completion.

time.note: Archive author index lists the message as "Fri May 03 2002 - 16:38:46 MDT" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky".

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: Racing to be first improves the outcome. Closest SL4 wording to the take itself: he endorses getting a Friendly AI built before a self-serving project. The 'other side' is a project building a self-serving AI, not a rival state, and the premise that the builder controls the outcome is not asserted. In 2002 he endorsed SIAI building a Friendly seed AI first; he did not claim the builder controls the outcome by default. Rejected explicitly in 2023: "anyone talking of arms races is a fool" (TIME), which does not refer back to these messages. "This" means designing Friendliness semantics for propaganda, i.e. an AI serving narrow goals. Cross-family check: holds the racing premise for a Friendly-first project; no located later text explicitly retracts that conditional strategy, so said-it rather than earlier-self.

claims.subject: extropians-2000-09-29-yudkowsky-6080
claims.statement: The Extropians message “Re: Eugene's nuclear threat” (2000-09-29) articulates Y24. Correcting his earlier post in a thread on Eugene Leitl's suggestion of nuclear strikes on AI facilities, he says the only things he can do are to write up Friendly AI and to try to be the first to build AI.

time.note: Archive author index lists the message as "Fri Sep 29 2000 - 11:43:19 MDT" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky".

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: Racing to be first improves the outcome. Being first is tied to writing up Friendly AI, not to beating a named rival; the same reply rejects coercion against other projects. Quotation kept short because the message has about 140 words of his own. Later rejections (his SL4 message of 2007-11-24: building an AI is pass-fail; TIME, 2023: 'anyone talking of arms races is a fool') do not refer back to this message. Earlier than his SL4 message of 2002-03-10. Cross-family check: not an earlier self, because no located later text explicitly retracts this Friendly-first strategy; recorded as said-it for the racing premise.

claims.subject: lw-2022-six-dimensions-of-operational-adequacy-in
claims.statement: The post “Six Dimensions of Operational Adequacy in AGI Projects” (2022-05-30) contests Y28. Introducing a list of properties a trustworthy AGI project would need, he says that no existing project qualifies.
claims.qualification: Premise addressed: A credible safety plan exists. The post's editor's note says it is a lightly edited copy of a document written in November 2017; posted 2022-05-30. Date the claim to 2017.

claimed.note: Editor's note says the document was written in November 2017; the wording is attested only in the lightly edited copy published 2022-05-30.

engagement.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage states the contrary conclusion without giving a reason against the premise that a credible safety plan exists, even when read with its message or dialogue turn.

claims.subject: lw-2008-that-tiny-note-of-discord
claims.statement: The post “That Tiny Note of Discord” (2008-09-23) bears on Y30. In an autobiographical series, he describes his late-1990s belief that a superintelligence would automatically do what was right, and in the same paragraph identifies the flaw in the argument he had built for it.

time.note: LessWrong postedAt of an imported Overcoming Bias post (Overcoming Bias date).

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: The default outcome is good. Imported Overcoming Bias post (2008-09-23), part of a retrospective sequence written in the third person about "Eliezer1997" and "Eliezer2000". The rejection is stated in the same paragraph ("The flaw being the unconsidered and unjustified equation of …"). The same paragraph names the flaw in the earlier belief; this is the later rejection, not his 2008 position. A 2008 retrospective reporting his earlier view; recorded as related, not earlier-self, because the earlier-self relation needs an earlier text that itself holds the take.

thought.missing: A 2008 report of his late-1990s belief that names its flaw; it does not hold that the default outcome is good.
